## Simple explanation

Optimization means searching for a good or best solution according to a
measurable goal. In machine learning, the goal is often to find model
parameters that make a loss function small.

## Technical explanation

An optimization problem specifies an objective and, optionally,
constraints. For model training, a common form is to minimize empirical
loss $L(\theta)$ over parameters $\theta$. The objective may be
non-convex, high-dimensional, and expensive to evaluate.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Training, hyperparameter selection, resource allocation, and scheduling
all involve optimization. The objective and constraints encode what the
system is intended to improve, so poorly chosen objectives can produce
solutions that score well numerically but fail in practice.

## How it works

An optimization algorithm proposes candidate values, evaluates the
objective, and updates its search based on previous results. Gradient-based
methods use derivatives where available; other problems use coordinate
search, evolutionary methods, or constrained solvers. Practical results
may be approximate and depend on initialization and computation limits.

## Practical example

During neural-network training, an optimizer updates weights to reduce
training loss. Engineers also monitor validation performance and resource
use, because optimizing training loss alone can lead to overfitting or
miss deployment constraints.

## Common misconceptions

- Optimization finds a solution relative to the specified objective, not automatically the best real-world outcome.
- A local optimum is not always a global optimum.
- Lower training loss does not guarantee better generalization.
